messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: We got our first GDPR erasure request, and it turns out Remove on the user
list doesn't remove anyone — it flips `active` off and scrambles the email,
and everything else stays.

Make it actually erase: nothing of theirs is left anywhere — not a row, not
a stale search hit. One exception: books they created that are shared with
everyone keep working — people are reading those. Take their name off and
byline them "Deleted author".

One wrinkle: most of the requests we owe are people someone already "removed"
the old way — deactivated, email rewritten to `alice-deactivated-<uuid>@...`.
It has to work for them too, and their sign-in log entries sit under the
address they actually signed in with.

After reviewing the schema, my next step would be to get a handle on the code structure. I'll need a comprehensive list of all the files. I'll start with the standard Rails directories: `app/models` to understand the data logic; `app/controllers` to get an idea of the user interaction; `app/jobs` to see any background processing being done, and maybe explore some key code flow paths. module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

    Redcarpet::Markdown.new(renderer, ActionText::Markdown::DEFAULT_MARKDOWN_EXTENSIONS)

  def searchable_content
    # `to_plain_text` decodes HTML entities, so characters like `<` that were `<`
    # in the original HTML become literal `<`. Re-encode them with `html_escape` so
    # they are safe in the FTS index. The `html_safe` return value signals to
    # `Leaf::Searchable#sanitize_for_index` that this content should not be

    ERB::Util.html_escape(plain_text)

  end

    def plain_text
      html_body = rendered_html(markdown_source)
      ActionText::Content.new(html_body).to_plain_text
    end

  end

module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

    renderer = Redcarpet::Render::HTML.new(ActionText::Markdown::DEFAULT_RENDERER_OPTIONS)

  end

  private
    def plain_text
      html_body = rendered_html(markdown_source)
      ActionText::Content.new(html_body).to_plain_text

require "test_helper"

class UsersControllerTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  setup do
    @join_code = accounts(:signal).join_code
  end

  test "new" do
    get join_url(@join_code)
    assert_response :success
  end

  test "new does not allow a signed in user" do
    sign_in :david

    get join_url(@join_code)
    assert_redirected_to root_url
  end

  test "new requires a join code" do
    get join_url("not")
    assert_response :not_found
  end

  test "create" do
    assert_difference -> { User.count }, 1 do
      post join_url(@join_code), params: { user: { name: "New Person", email_address: "new@example.com", password: "secret123456" } }
    end

    assert_redirected_to root_url

    user = User.last
    assert_equal user.id, Session.find_by(token: parsed_cookies.signed[:session_token]).user.id
  end

  test "creating a new user with an existing email address redirects to login screen" do
    assert_no_difference -> { User.count } do
      post join_url(@join_code), params: { user: { name: "Another David", email_address: users(:david).email_address, password: "secret123456" } }
    end

    assert_redirected_to new_session_url(email_address: users(:david).email_address)
  end

  test "update" do
    sign_in :david
    assert users(:david).administrator?

    put user_url(users(:kevin)), params: { user: { role: "administrator" } }

    assert_redirected_to users_url
    assert users(:kevin).reload.administrator?
  end

  test "update does not allow non-admins to change roles" do
    sign_in :kevin
    assert_not users(:kevin).administrator?

    put user_url(users(:kevin)), params: { user: { role: "administrator" } }

    assert_response :forbidden
    assert_not users(:kevin).reload.administrator?
  end

  test "destroy" do
    sign_in :david

    assert_difference -> { User.active.count }, -1 do
      delete user_url(users(:kevin))
    end

    assert_redirected_to users_url
    assert_nil User.active.find_by(id: users(:kevin).id)
  end

  test "destroy is not allowed to non-admins" do
    sign_in :kevin

    delete user_url(users(:david))
    assert_response :forbidden
  end
end

require "test_helper"

class BookTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "slug is generated from title" do
    book = Book.create!(title: "Hello, World!")
    assert_equal "hello-world", book.slug
  end

  test "press a leafable" do
    leaf = books(:manual).press Page.new(body: "Important words"), title: "Introduction"

    assert leaf.page?
    assert_equal "Important words", leaf.page.body.content.to_s
    assert_equal "Introduction", leaf.title
  end

  test "markable combines all leafables" do
    leaves(:welcome_page).leafable.update!(body: "Welcome page content")
    leaves(:summary_page).leafable.update!(body: "Summary page content")

    assert_includes books(:handbook).markable, "Welcome page content"
    assert_includes books(:handbook).markable, "Summary page content"
  end

  test "markable joins leafables with double newlines" do
    leaves(:welcome_page).leafable.update!(body: "Welcome content")
    leaves(:summary_page).leafable.update!(body: "Summary content")

    assert_includes books(:handbook).markable, "Welcome content\n\nSummary content"
  end

  test "markable only includes active leaves" do
    leaves(:welcome_page).leafable.update!(body: "Active content")
    leaves(:summary_page).trashed!

    assert_includes books(:handbook).markable, "Active content"
    assert_not_includes books(:handbook).markable, leaves(:summary_page).title
  end

  test "markable returns empty string for book with no leaves" do
    assert_equal "", books(:manual).markable
  end
end

**GDPR Erasure: A Deep Dive into the Requirements and Implementation**

Okay, let's break this down meticulously. First, the core problem: the current "Remove" functionality is a misnomer. It deactivates users and obscures their email, but it doesn't truly erase their data, violating GDPR. Now, the goal is clear: implement *actual* erasure, with the defined exception of shared books.

First, I need to analyze the current system. The front-end view, `app/views/users/_user.html.erb`, confirms that the button already gives the user the impression that data is permanently deleted. The `UsersController#destroy` action, however, shows that the data is not being deleted, but the user is being deactivated through a call to `@user.deactivate`! This is the core discrepancy.

Crucially, `UsersController#set_user` uses `User.active.find(params[:id])`, which means *already deactivated users* are not included in search results and can't be found through the current route, which is a major issue. This immediately creates a conflict: the prompt states that the erasure mechanism must work on *already deactivated* users.

Now, let's explore all possible interaction points for removal:

1.  **`DELETE /users/:id`**: Currently, this route will return a 404 for deactivated users because of the `set_user` method. The `update` route is probably designed to work only on active users.
2.  **UI through `users/index.html.erb`**: If deactivated users aren't shown, a user can't be removed through this UI flow! Is that correct?
3.  **Direct `user.destroy` / `user.erase` via model/console/rake task**: Are deactivated users able to be directly erased, and if so, how?

The `UsersController#index` action further complicates this, as `@users = User.active`, meaning deactivated users aren't even listed! This is a core design decision.

Now, let's carefully consider two potential approaches:

**Possibility A**: In `UsersController#destroy`, `set_user` could be updated to `User.find(params[:id])` (not `User.active.find`), allowing the destruction route to process already deactivated users. The `User#destroy` or `User#erase` action in the model would need to be re-evaluated to work on either active or deactivated users, or there will need to be new code.

**Possibility B**: What if the deactivated users are not supposed to be visible in the user list? Are they still accessible through a different action, or is there a different way for the admin/system to remove them?

I need to confirm existing tests for `/users`, the `users/_user.html.erb` partial, and how `User.active` is used, so I have to analyze these cases, along with the current flow and logic, by searching existing test files.

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive into Data Erasure for a User**

Alright, let's break down this data erasure process. We need to be absolutely certain we're scrubbing everything related to a user, and, critically, handle those legacy deactivated users with their potentially altered email addresses.

First, the core: the `users` table. The goal is complete deletion; no trace left. That means a hard delete for the `users` row.

Next, the `sessions` table. Here's where it gets interesting. The `User` has `has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy`. But wait! There's `Session::Auditable`. `after_destroy :record_signed_out` in `Session::Auditable` is triggered when a session is destroyed! And guess what that does? It *creates* a `SignInEvent` row! That's a huge problem. If we just do a straight `user.destroy` we'll get a `SignInEvent` being created after we're trying to erase the user. So, we must avoid triggering this.

The initial thought was to use `sessions.delete_all` in a `before_destroy` hook, which would bypass the callbacks, but now I'm thinking, that might not be enough. The `sessions` could be destroyed *after* we delete `sign_in_events`, leading to a race condition and a stray `SignInEvent` row. Ideally we should do *both*, destroy the sessions *before* deleting sign in events to avoid the signed_out event. or just use `sessions.delete_all`

The goal is absolute data hygiene. When a user is erased, there should be no sign-out events generated. We need to use `sessions.delete_all` *or* delete `sign_in_events` after destroying sessions (or both) to ensure no `SignInEvent` remains after erasure.

Now, `sign_in_events`. This is where the legacy deactivated users come in. These users might have `email_address` values with those nasty "deactivated" prefixes: `alice-deactivated-<uuid>@example.com`. The key is to correctly identify the original email address, which can be done by stripping the `"-deactivated-<uuid>"` part, leaving the original email. However, we must be careful. We need to handle this pattern: `email_address.sub(/-deactivated-[^@]+@/, "@")`. It's crucial this only applies to deactivated users (`!active?`), to not match an active user whose address contains `-deactivated-`.

Also, what if someone was deactivated multiple times? If the email has a double `-deactivated-` prefix, the regex would only remove the first one, but since only deactivated users need this stripping, we can do it by using `sub(/-deactivated-[^@]+@/, "@")`. However, that will not work if we try to erase a user with an invalid deactivated email, like `alice-deactivated-uuid@example.com`.

We *must* handle edge cases. Test values. Potentially, a user *could* have been deactivated multiple times, with their email address mangled repeatedly.

So, in summary, to erase a user completely:

1.  We need to *ensure* no `SignInEvent` rows are left behind.
2.  `sessions.delete_all` (or deleting `sign_in_events` *after* sessions are destroyed, or ideally, both).
3.  For deactivated users (`!active?`), we need to grab the original email address by stripping the deactivated prefix using the regex `email_address.sub(/-deactivated-[^@]+@/, "@")`.
4.  We must make sure that sign-in events are queried, case insensitively, using both the current address and the original email address, if `!active?`.
5.  Search the entire repo for all uses of email_address to ensure that our assumptions are correct.

This whole process should be done with extreme care.

**Deep Dive into User Deletion and Data Integrity**

Alright, let's break down this user deactivation and deletion process. Initially, the `email_address` field seems clean, directly reflecting the user's email, stored with `SignInEvent.for_address`. But the real challenge lies in handling email changes and deactivations gracefully, without leaving stale data. The `deactivate` method modifies the email address to include a UUID, making it `alice-deactivated-<uuid>@example.com`, while `SignInEvent` stores the original. The strategy seems to be reversing this deactivation with regex to match either a UUID or any "deactivated" tag. If the email has the correct deactivated pattern, we first try to restore the email to the format using the UUID pattern and fall back to a simpler pattern if there's no UUID and the user isn't active. This ensures we can get back the original email even if a user has been deactivated multiple times or entered a malformed email. This will then restore the original email address, which is then used to find existing Sign in Events to delete. However, this raises questions about edge cases, like testing with manually created deactivated users, or double-deactivated emails where we should match using the UUID.

The most crucial concern is preventing sign-in events from active users getting deleted! If someone signs in with an email after a previous user was deactivated and that account is then deleted, we must be careful not to delete any active users sign in events! To prevent this, only restore email addresses if the user is deactivated. We also need to be careful when cleaning up sign in events and double check that the current email is not an active user. The goal seems to be to delete all associated sign-in events for a deactivated user unless the email is now active by another user, and this could be verified. Tests need to be carefully constructed to ensure the right events are deleted, and no active user's sign-in events get removed.

Now, let's move beyond the `users` table and check every other table in the database schema.

Here's the inventory:
*   `accounts`: account-level data (no user reference).
*   `users`: the primary user data.
*   `sessions`: linked to `users` via `user_id`, no cascade delete.
*   `sign_in_events`: stores email addresses. No foreign key, deletion via the method described above.
*   `accesses`: `user_id` -> `users.id`, no cascade delete.
*   `reading_marks`: `user_id` -> `users.id`, no cascade delete!

That last one is a potential problem. Inspecting `User::Authoring`, reveals `has_many :reading_marks` *without* `dependent: :destroy` or `dependent: :delete_all`. This means that if we call `user.destroy` (or `delete`) on a user with `reading_marks`, the deletion will fail due to a foreign key constraint violation. We must add `dependent: :delete_all` (or `destroy`). We can add this to the `user` table.

*   `books`: `creator_id` -> `users.id`, no cascade delete.

Regarding `books`, the prompt dictates that publicly shared books should be retained even after the creator is gone, but the creator's name should be replaced with "Deleted author." Let's confirm that these "publicly shared books" correspond to books where `everyone_access` is `true`. We should then query the book table, where the creator id equals the current user, and set the creator to null, and the author to deleted author.

We need to confirm the terminology:
*   `everyone_access`:boolean, default `true`.
*   `published`: boolean.

We need to review how these are used in the application. We should grep for terms across the code to solidify our understanding of these flags.

**Analyzing Transactional Behavior in Search Indexing**

Okay, here's the deal. I've been digging into how we're handling search index updates and deletions, especially within transactions. The output from the test runs confirms my suspicions. When using `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index`, the search index (`leaf_search_index`) *doesn't* get updated immediately inside a transactional context. This means that in both transactional tests and potentially in production scenarios with nested transactions, the index still contains the deleted row until the outermost transaction commits.

The potential for stale search hits is significant. Consider the scenario where `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index, if: :searchable?` is used. If the `leafable` object's searchable content becomes empty or `nil` *before* the `after_destroy_commit` hook fires, the index won't be updated, leading to stale data. The same applies to a Section object when the body is updated to `""` or `nil`.

However, the real key is the database. Since we're using SQLite, `leaf_search_index` is in the same database as our other tables. If we use `after_destroy :remove_from_search_index` instead of `after_destroy_commit`, then the index row is deleted *within* the transaction, guaranteeing atomicity. This means that if the transaction commits, both the data and the index row are deleted. If it rolls back, both are restored. This makes things predictable both in production and in our transactional tests! And removing the `if: :searchable?` condition ensures that *any* leaf gets its search index row deleted, even if `searchable_content` is now empty.

Now, let's circle back to the prompt's request to "erase" everything, specifically the concern about "stale search hits".

There are two primary ways a stale search hit can occur:
1.  In transactional tests: If a row is present in the `leaf_search_index` table after a `destroy`, it may be returned via direct search queries against the `leaf_search_index` table or through `Leaf.search(...)`.
2.  In FTS5 (the likely database) the content may be stored in the index table itself, not linked via row id, and thus not cleaned up in the case of a `delete_all` or other non-`after_destroy_commit` cases.

By using `after_destroy :remove_from_search_index` (unconditionally), with SQLite FTS5, the index gets cleaned up *immediately* and atomically with the deletion of the data rows, addressing both scenarios.

However, the `Leaf::Searchable` module's `create_in_search_index` and `update_in_search_index` use `after_create_commit` and `after_update_commit` respectively. It's time to check if we can remove or refactor those since they may be causing issues with tests. A quick look at `searchable_test.rb` and `searches_controller_test.rb` is needed.

The `searchable_test.rb` had a test where we called `pages(:welcome).update! body: "sausages"` and expected the search index to update and, thankfully, it did. This is likely because the `Page` model has `has_one :leaf, touch: true`, and the `Leaf` model uses `after_update_commit :update_in_search_index`. This triggers an `after_update_commit` callback, and it worked in our test.

A quick note on why `after_destroy_commit` *didn't* work in the `rails runner` but the `after_update_commit` worked in the test: in Rails 7/8, `TestFixtures` uses `connection.begin_transaction(joinable: false)`. When `joinable: false`, the `transaction do ... end` inside `ActiveRecord` creates a REAL savepoint, and Rails' `TransactionManager` fires `after_commit` (and other hooks) when the savepoint finishes. In contrast, in the `rails runner` scenario, we used `ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do ... end` *without* `joinable: false`, so the inner transaction joined the outer transaction, which is why the hooks didn't fire in the test.

I'll check the behavior with `joinable: false` and test in Minitest as well to confirm.

**Major Discoveries and Consequent Investigations**

Okay, wow, let's break this down. That output is... enlightening. First, the data before and after the `book.destroy!` call: I see some concerning behavior here. Notably, `Pages` and `ActionText::Markdown` dropped from 2 to 1. That *shouldn't* happen. My initial thought is to check the fixtures for the baseline count, which is only 2 Pages. But why did those numbers change at all?

Looking closer, I realize the `Page` and `ActionText::Markdown` entries are being orphaned. The `Edit` revisions are pointing to old, now-destroyed, records. This is a HUGE problem! I see that `Leaf::Editable` uses `dependent: :delete_all` on `edits`. This is the crux of the issue: because `delete_all` doesn't trigger callbacks (like `destroy`), any dependent records—`Page`, `Section`, `Picture`, and `ActionText::Markdown` for each edit—are left dangling in the database. This violates the prompt! We're supposed to be *erasing* everything, not leaving stale data behind.

The next concern, which is related to the previous point, is that `Edit` has a `delegated_type` relationship with `leafable` set to `dependent: :destroy`. So, let's explore if `dependent: :destroy` on both `Leaf` and `Edit` create a double destruction, and if the system handles that cleanly.

The second major finding relates to `ActiveStorage::Blob` and that 3 remains after the destroy. Why? Because the `purge_later` on the `cover` attachment, and default `purge_later` on the `image` attachment in `Picture` is *enqueueing* the purge job, not executing it synchronously. My testing environment probably uses an async queue adapter, which is why the `Blobs` are still there. Only the `Attachment` rows are deleted. I need to verify that `has_many_attached ..., dependent: :destroy` will still enqueue the job, or if it will do the purge synchronously. If the purge job is not run, this is another major data leakage issue.

I'm starting to see a pattern here, and it all revolves around how dependencies are handled. I need to dig into the `config/environments/*.rb` to check the queue settings and do some careful testing with `rails runner` to verify my assumptions about `Edit` and `dependent: :destroy`, as well as to check if the `ActiveStorage` purges run synchronously. Let's see if we can trigger the purges manually.

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing Active Storage Purging Strategies for Robust Data Cleanup**

Okay, let's break this down for secure data deletion, considering Active Storage and the application's specific setup. My primary goal is to ensure all associated data is purged correctly when a user's private books and their related content (images, Markdown uploads, edits) are erased.

First, the `ActiveStorage::Blob#purge` method...it's crucial to understand it rescues `ActiveRecord::InvalidForeignKey`.  Then, there's `ActiveStorage::Blob.unattached`. It finds blobs that have no attachments left, a great starting point for clean-up.

Now, considering the application's structure: `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` uses `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy`, which is good.  `Book` uses `has_one_attached :cover, dependent: :purge_later`, and `Picture` defaults to `:purge_later` for its image.  This `:purge_later` is a key consideration.

Here's my approach: When we erase a user's private books, I'll collect all blob IDs associated with them (cover images, picture images, markdown uploads, and even those in edit leafables). Then, after destroying the books, I'll use `ActiveStorage::Blob.unattached.where(id: blob_ids).find_each(&:purge)`—or should it be `purge_later`?  The goal is to purge only the unattached blobs. This has to be *after* the destruction of the books. Wait! It looks like using `purge` deletes everything *immediately*. The blob, the variant records, and the files on disk! This seems perfect for immediate cleanup, leaving no orphaned data.

Let me check `ActiveStorage::VariantRecord`! Good. In Rails, `ActiveStorage::Blob` has `has_many :variant_records, dependent: :destroy`. So `blob.purge` handles deleting those variant records *and* the files.

Now, the transactional aspect is critical. The comment in `blob.rb` warns against using `purge` within a transaction. But our storage is local (disk), not S3.  So, `blob.purge` is very fast, just deleting a local file. That changes things. We can run `purge` immediately after `destroy`, or in `after_destroy_commit`.  In a transactional test, `after_destroy_commit` only runs if there is no joinable transaction! Since our tests use local storage, `blob.purge` is instant and guaranteed to remove the blob rows in tests, even those that don't do background jobs!

Next, `Leaf::Editable` and `Edit`. Let's examine those models carefully! I see `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` in `Leaf::Editable`. This means when a `Leaf` is destroyed, only the `edits` rows are deleted, leaving behind the `Page`, `Section`, `Picture`, `ActionText::Markdown`, and `ActiveStorage::Attachment` data from past revisions.

What if we changed it to `has_many :edits, dependent: :destroy`?  Let's consider two cases where `leaf.destroy!` runs:

*   **Case 1:** A `Leaf` with a current `leafable` (e.g., `page_curr`) and one revision edit (`edit1` -> `page_old`). If `has_many :edits, dependent: :destroy`, destroying the leaf will destroy both the current leafable and the old leafable and all the associated data. This is what we want.

*   **Case 2:** A trashed `leaf` with a `trash` edit (`edit2` -> `page_curr`, the *same* as the current leafable!). We need to test the interaction if `has_many :edits, dependent: :destroy` when `edit2.leafable == leaf.leafable`. This is critical! A `rails runner` test will be necessary to confirm the behavior.

**Analyzing Active Storage Purging Strategies**

Okay, so I'm thinking about how to handle Active Storage attachments when we're dealing with destroying a bunch of "private" books. It seems like the existing setup doesn't explicitly call `PurgeJob` for every single attachment, which raises a flag. We need to be careful! We already know `BooksController#remove_cover` calls `@book.cover.purge` synchronously, but that might be the only place.

My immediate thought is to trace the execution path when `User::Authoring` (or just `User`) collects all the `blob_ids` associated with these `private_books` (those with `everyone_access: false`), destroys the books themselves, and then purges any leftover, unattached blobs. Sounds like a good plan.

Let's see, the core is collecting `blob_ids` efficiently. What can have attachments *inside* a `Book`? I need to build this out clearly and cleanly.

*   `Book#cover` – that's straightforward: use `ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "Book", record_id: book_ids)`.
*   `Picture#image` – both the current `leaf.leafable` *and* the `edit.leafable` versions. So, we'll need to figure out `picture_ids` and then fetch attachments using `ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "Picture", record_id: picture_ids)`.
*   `ActionText::Markdown#uploads` – this also applies to *both* current `Page#body` and `edit.leafable` `Page#body`. So, we will need to figure out `markdown_ids` and then fetch attachments using `ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "ActionText::Markdown", record_id: markdown_ids)`.

This looks like it can be elegantly SQL-backed, which is ideal! Let's lay it out, assuming we have a `book` or a set of `book_ids`:

1.  `leaf_ids = Leaf.where(book_id: book_ids).pluck(:id)` (or a subquery if needed).
2.  `leafable_pairs` from `Leaf.where(book_id: book_ids)` and `Edit.where(leaf_id: leaf_ids)`
3.  Calculate `picture_ids` and `page_ids` from those leaves and edits.
4.  `markdown_ids = ActionText::Markdown.where(record_type: "Page", record_id: page_ids).select(:id)`.
5.  `blob_ids = ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "Book", record_id: book_ids).or(ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "Picture", record_id: picture_ids)).or(ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "ActionText::Markdown", record_id: markdown_ids)).distinct.pluck(:blob_id)`.

Then, *after* we `private_books.destroy_all`, we can run: `ActiveStorage::Blob.unattached.where(id: blob_ids).find_each(&:purge)`!

Now I'm remembering – what happens if `dependent: :purge_later` *also* enqueues a `PurgeJob`? That's the critical question.

In production, using something like Resque, `PurgeJob` executes `blob.purge`. If the blob has already been deleted because of the synchronous purge, `ActiveJob` deserializes the `GlobalID`, which then leads to an `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` error. But, critically, the `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` should have `discard_on ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`. So, that prevents those errors from piling up! Let's double check that in the Rails gem, to be sure.

If the `shared_book` is kept, the `ReadingMark` shouldn't be deleted via `shared_leaf` deletion, and Rails SQLite3 should fail due to `ActiveRecord::InvalidForeignKey` if `PRAGMA foreign_keys` is on (which it should be by default).

name: Build and publish container image to GHCR

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    tags:
      - 'v*'
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: publish-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions: {}

env:
  IMAGE_DESCRIPTION: Instantly publish your own books on the web for free, no publisher required.
  SOURCE_URL: https://github.com/${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  build:
    name: Build and push image (${{ matrix.arch }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    timeout-minutes: 45
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - runner: ubuntu-latest
            platform: linux/amd64
            arch: amd64
          - runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm
            platform: linux/arm64
            arch: arm64
    env:
      REGISTRY: ghcr.io
      IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@bb05f3f5519dd87d3ba754cc423b652a5edd6d2c # v4.2.0

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@c99871dec2022cc055c062a10cc1a1310835ceb4 # v4.3.0
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Compute canonical image name (lowercase)
        id: vars
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -eu
          IMAGE_REF="${IMAGE_NAME:-$GITHUB_REPOSITORY}"
          CANONICAL_IMAGE="${REGISTRY}/${IMAGE_REF,,}"
          echo "canonical=${CANONICAL_IMAGE}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          if [[ "${GITHUB_REF}" == refs/tags/v* ]]; then
            APP_VERSION="${GITHUB_REF#refs/tags/v}"
          else
            APP_VERSION="${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
          fi
          echo "app_version=${APP_VERSION}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Extract Docker metadata (tags, labels) with arch suffix
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@dc802804100637a589fabce1cb79ff13a1411302 # v6.2.0
        with:
          images: ${{ steps.vars.outputs.canonical }}
          tags: |
            type=ref,event=branch
            type=ref,event=tag
            type=sha,format=short,prefix=sha-
            type=semver,pattern={{version}},enable=${{ startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v') }}
            type=semver,pattern={{major}}.{{minor}},enable=${{ startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v') }}
            type=semver,pattern={{major}},enable=${{ startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v') }}
          flavor: |
            latest=false
            suffix=-${{ matrix.arch }}
          labels: |
            org.opencontainers.image.source=${{ env.SOURCE_URL }}

      - name: Build and push (${{ matrix.platform }})
        id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@53b7df96c91f9c12dcc8a07bcb9ccacbed38856a # v7.3.0
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          build-args: |
            OCI_SOURCE=${{ env.SOURCE_URL }}
            OCI_DESCRIPTION=${{ env.IMAGE_DESCRIPTION }}

  def deactivate

module User::Authoring
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  DELETED_AUTHOR_BYLINE = "Deleted author"

  included do
    has_many :created_books, class_name: "Book", foreign_key: :creator_id,
      inverse_of: :creator, dependent: :destroy

    has_many :reading_marks, dependent: :delete_all

    before_destroy :prepare_created_books_for_erasure, prepend: true
    after_destroy :purge_erased_blobs
  end

    def prepare_created_books_for_erasure
      created_books.with_everyone_access.find_each do |book|
        book.update!(creator: nil, author: DELETED_AUTHOR_BYLINE)
      end

      private_book_ids = created_books.where(everyone_access: false).pluck(:id)
      @erased_blob_ids = blob_ids_for_books(private_book_ids)
      created_books.reset
    end

    def purge_erased_blobs
      return if @erased_blob_ids.blank?

      ActiveStorage::Blob.unattached.where(id: @erased_blob_ids).find_each(&:purge)
    end

    def blob_ids_for_books(book_ids)

      leaf_ids = Leaf.where(book_id: book_ids).select(:id)
      leaves_scope = Leaf.where(id: leaf_ids)
      edits_scope = Edit.where(leaf_id: leaf_ids)

      page_ids = leaves_scope.where(leafable_type: "Page").pluck(:leafable_id) +
        edits_scope.where(leafable_type: "Page").pluck(:leafable_id)

        .or(ActiveStorage::Attachment.where(record_type: "ActionText::Markdown", record_id: markdown_ids))
        .distinct
        .pluck(:blob_id)
    end
end
